Denmark Defense Leaders Take Serious View of Flying Saucers

The report discuss sighting of Flying Saucers in 1952 over Karup Air Base in Denmark. Unidentified Drones/UFOs were again sighted in 2025 over the same base, 73 years later – this is no coincidence.

#ufotwitter

The document is a declassified CIA report dating from July 4, 1953, containing an English translation (or summary) of an article originally published in Copenhagen on 12 July 1953 in leading Danish newspapers. It was circulated within the U.S. intelligence community.

Danish Military Takes the Phenomenon Seriously:

Danish defense authorities — particularly experts from the Danish Air Force Command — regarded flying saucers (unidentified aerial phenomena) as a problem worthy of serious attention, not just public curiosity.

Official Report Based on Radar and Observer Reports:

The Danish Air Force had compiled a report for the Defense Staff summarizing air observations over Denmark and adjacent waters. This report included data from air force radar stations and sightings by trained observers.

Comparison With Other Scandinavian and Soviet Activity:

Danish military analysts compared these sightings with other reports from Norway and Finland, including objects that might be linked to remote-controlled projectiles or unknown aircraft. Based on this, some military personnel speculated that the unidentified objects could be coming from a Soviet base in the Arctic — specifically Novaya Zemlya.

Specific Sightings Mentioned:

The text describes an incident at Karup Airfield in Jutland (12 November 1952) where an officer and seven privates observed a craft that resembled an aircraft but moved much faster than any known Danish plane. Other Scandinavian sightings are also referenced, such as a mysterious object seen during a Swedish maneuver that a jet couldn’t intercept.

Military Interest and Implications:

The Danish Defense Intelligence Service and Air Force Command considered these observations of ”flying saucer traffic” to be of significant aerotechnical interest, meaning they might have implications for air defense and military operations — not merely public anecdotes.
